title: Abraham smashes the idols
summary: In Genesis Rabbah, Abraham smashes the idols in his father's shop, blames the largest one, and is thrown into a furnace by Nimrod. In the Quran, Abraham breaks the idols except the biggest, tells the people to ask them, and is thrown into a fire made cool.

title: The Buddha becomes a Christian saint
summary: The life of the Buddha passed through Manichaean and Arabic versions (Bilawhar wa-Būdhāsf) into the Georgian Balavariani and the Greek Barlaam and Ioasaph. Josaphat became a saint in the Christian calendar.

evidence.text: The name chain bodhisattva → Būdhāsaf → Yūdāsaf → Iōasaph is the lexical spine of the lead.

title: The raven that teaches burial
summary: In the Quran a raven shows Cain how to bury Abel. In Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer a raven shows Adam and Eve.

passages.text: فَبَعَثَ ٱللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ لِيُرِيَهُۥ كَيْفَ يُوَٰرِى سَوْءَةَ أَخِيهِ قَالَ يَٰوَيْلَتَىٰٓ أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَٰذَا ٱلْغُرَابِ فَأُوَٰرِىَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِى فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ ٱلنَّٰدِمِينَ

evidence.text: Who learns from the raven differs (Cain vs. Adam). Dating PRE relative to the Quran is part of the question.

title: Jesus brings clay birds to life
summary: In the Infancy Gospel of Thomas the child Jesus shapes sparrows from clay and makes them fly. The Quran has Jesus fashion birds from clay that become birds by God's permission.

passages.text: (3:49) وَرَسُولًا إِلَىٰ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ أَنِّى قَدْ جِئْتُكُم بِـَٔايَةٍ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ أَنِّىٓ أَخْلُقُ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ فَأَنفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَأُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ وَأُحْىِ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا تَأْكُلُونَ وَمَا تَدَّخِرُونَ فِى بُيُوتِكُمْ إِنَّ فِى ذَٰلِكَ لَءَايَةً لَّكُمْ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ (5:110) إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ ٱذْكُرْ نِعْمَتِى عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَىٰ وَٰلِدَتِكَ إِذْ أَيَّدتُّكَ بِرُوحِ ٱلْقُدُسِ تُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ فِى ٱلْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلًا وَإِذْ عَلَّمْتُكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ وَٱلتَّوْرَىٰةَ وَٱلْإِنجِيلَ وَإِذْ تَخْلُقُ مِنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ بِإِذْنِى فَتَنفُخُ فِيهَا فَتَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِى وَتُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ بِإِذْنِى وَإِذْ تُخْرِجُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِى وَإِذْ كَفَفْتُ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ عَنكَ إِذْ جِئْتَهُم بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ فَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ مِنْهُمْ إِنْ هَٰذَآ إِلَّا سِحْرٌ مُّبِينٌ

evidence.text: The Quran adds 'by God's permission' (bi-idhnī), which reframes the miracle theologically. That is a response-type detail.

title: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Alexander legends
summary: The Quran's Dhul-Qarnayn travels to where the sun sets and rises and builds a barrier against Gog and Magog. The Syriac Alexander Legend and the Alexander Romance have close parallels.

evidence.text: The Syriac Legend is often dated around 630 (Reinink), close to the Quran. The direction and the dating are both debated.

title: Flood narratives across traditions
summary: A divinely sent flood with a chosen survivor appears in Sumerian, Akkadian, Hebrew, Quranic, Vedic, Greek, and Chinese sources. The Near Eastern versions are historically linked; the others are candidate convergences.

passages.text_omitted: longer than 12 verses; read it in the source

passages.ref: Shujing; Mencius (Gun and Yu tame the flood)

evidence.text: Specificity test: the bird-release sequence (Gilgamesh XI; Genesis 8) is a rare motif combination that marks the Mesopotamian–Hebrew link. The Quran has no bird release.
Noah's drowned son (Quran 11:42–43) has no Genesis counterpart and is a sub-lead.
The Chinese story is about controlling the flood, not surviving it, so it is a weak match.

title: Han Kitab: Islam in Neo-Confucian terms
summary: Chinese Muslim scholars such as Wang Daiyu and Liu Zhi expressed tawḥīd with Neo-Confucian metaphysics: 真一 'the Real One', li and qi, and the Supreme Ultimate, in dialogue with Zhu Xi.

passages.ref: Zhu Xi, commentaries; Zhou Dunyi, Taijitu shuo

title: haykal: the Sumerian 'big house'
summary: Sumerian é-gal ('big house', palace) became Akkadian ekallu, Hebrew hêkhāl (palace, temple), Aramaic hêkhlā, and Arabic haykal.

evidence.text: haykal does not occur in the Quran; it is a control case for the lexical track.

title: ʼâçôwn: a word shared by Joseph and Moses
summary: אָסוֹן (ʼâçôwn, H611) occurs in 5 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Joseph (3) and Moses (2). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וְאֶת בִּנְיָמִין֙ אֲחִ֣י יוֹסֵ֔ף לֹא שָׁלַ֥ח יַעֲקֹ֖ב אֶת אֶחָ֑יו כִּ֣י אָמַ֔ר פֶּן יִקְרָאֶ֖נּוּ אָסֽוֹן
וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לֹֽא יֵרֵ֥ד בְּנִ֖י עִמָּכֶ֑ם כִּֽי אָחִ֨יו מֵ֜ת וְה֧וּא לְבַדּ֣וֹ נִשְׁאָ֗ר וּקְרָאָ֤הוּ אָסוֹן֙ בַּדֶּ֨רֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֵּֽלְכוּ בָ֔הּ וְהוֹרַדְתֶּ֧ם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִ֛י בְּיָג֖וֹן שְׁאֽוֹלָה
וּלְקַחְתֶּ֧ם גַּם אֶת זֶ֛ה מֵעִ֥ם פָּנַ֖י וְקָרָ֣הוּ אָס֑וֹן וְהֽוֹרַדְתֶּ֧ם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִ֛י בְּרָעָ֖ה שְׁאֹֽלָה
וְכִֽי יִנָּצ֣וּ אֲנָשִׁ֗ים וְנָ֨גְפ֜וּ אִשָּׁ֤ה הָרָה֙ וְיָצְא֣וּ יְלָדֶ֔יהָ וְלֹ֥א יִהְיֶ֖ה אָס֑וֹן עָנ֣וֹשׁ יֵעָנֵ֗שׁ כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׁ֤ית עָלָיו֙ בַּ֣עַל הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה וְנָתַ֖ן בִּפְלִלִֽים
וְאִם אָס֖וֹן יִהְיֶ֑ה וְנָתַתָּ֥ה נֶ֖פֶשׁ תַּ֥חַת נָֽפֶשׁ

title: bᵉkîyrâh: a word shared by Jacob and Saul
summary: בְּכִירָה (bᵉkîyrâh, H1067) occurs in 6 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Jacob (1) and Saul (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וַתֹּ֧אמֶר הַבְּכִירָ֛ה אֶל הַצְּעִירָ֖ה אָבִ֣ינוּ זָקֵ֑ן וְאִ֨ישׁ אֵ֤ין בָּאָ֨רֶץ֙ לָב֣וֹא עָלֵ֔ינוּ כְּדֶ֖רֶךְ כָּל הָאָֽרֶץ
וַתַּשְׁקֶ֧יןָ אֶת אֲבִיהֶ֛ן יַ֖יִן בַּלַּ֣יְלָה ה֑וּא וַתָּבֹ֤א הַבְּכִירָה֙ וַתִּשְׁכַּ֣ב אֶת אָבִ֔יהָ וְלֹֽא יָדַ֥ע בְּשִׁכְבָ֖הּ וּבְקׄוּמָֽהּ
וַֽיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת וַתֹּ֤אמֶר הַבְּכִירָה֙ אֶל הַצְּעִירָ֔ה הֵן שָׁכַ֥בְתִּי אֶ֖מֶשׁ אֶת אָבִ֑י נַשְׁקֶ֨נּוּ יַ֜יִן גַּם הַלַּ֗יְלָה וּבֹ֨אִי֙ שִׁכְבִ֣י עִמּ֔וֹ וּנְחַיֶּ֥ה מֵאָבִ֖ינוּ זָֽרַע
וַתֵּ֤לֶד הַבְּכִירָה֙ בֵּ֔ן וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ מוֹאָ֑ב ה֥וּא אֲבִֽי מוֹאָ֖ב עַד הַיּֽוֹם
וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָבָ֔ן לֹא יֵעָשֶׂ֥ה כֵ֖ן בִּמְקוֹמֵ֑נוּ לָתֵ֥ת הַצְּעִירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַבְּכִירָֽה
וַיִּֽהְיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י שָׁא֔וּל יוֹנָתָ֥ן וְיִשְׁוִ֖י וּמַלְכִּי שׁ֑וּעַ וְשֵׁם֙ שְׁתֵּ֣י בְנֹתָ֔יו שֵׁ֤ם הַבְּכִירָה֙ מֵרַ֔ב וְשֵׁ֥ם הַקְּטַנָּ֖ה מִיכַֽל

title: bᵉsôwrâh: a word shared by David and Elisha
summary: בְּשׂוֹרָה (bᵉsôwrâh, H1309) occurs in 6 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: David (5) and Elisha (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: כִּ֣י הַמַּגִּיד֩ לִ֨י לֵאמֹ֜ר הִנֵּה מֵ֣ת שָׁא֗וּל וְהֽוּא הָיָ֤ה כִמְבַשֵּׂר֙ בְּעֵינָ֔יו וָאֹחֲזָ֣ה ב֔וֹ וָאֶהְרְגֵ֖הוּ בְּצִֽקְלָ֑ג אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְתִתִּי ל֖וֹ בְּשֹׂרָֽה
וַיֹּ֧אמֶר ל֣וֹ יוֹאָ֗ב לֹא֩ אִ֨ישׁ בְּשֹׂרָ֤ה אַתָּה֙ הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה וּבִשַּׂרְתָּ֖ בְּי֣וֹם אַחֵ֑ר וְהַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ לֹ֣א תְבַשֵּׂ֔ר כִּֽי על עַל כֵּ֥ן בֶּן הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מֵֽת

וַיֹּ֨סֶף ע֜וֹד אֲחִימַ֤עַץ בֶּן צָדוֹק֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל יוֹאָ֔ב וִ֣יהִי מָ֔ה אָרֻֽצָה נָּ֥א גַם אָ֖נִי אַחֲרֵ֣י הַכּוּשִׁ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֗ב לָֽמָּה זֶּ֞ה אַתָּ֥ה רָץ֙ בְּנִ֔י וּלְכָ֖ה אֵין בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה מֹצֵֽאת
וַיִּקְרָ֤א הַצֹּפֶה֙ וַיַּגֵּ֣ד לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אִם לְבַדּ֖וֹ בְּשׂוֹרָ֣ה בְּפִ֑יו וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ הָל֖וֹךְ וְקָרֵֽב
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַצֹּפֶ֔ה אֲנִ֤י רֹאֶה֙ אֶת מְרוּצַ֣ת הָרִאשׁ֔וֹן כִּמְרֻצַ֖ת אֲחִימַ֣עַץ בֶּן צָד֑וֹק וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אִֽישׁ ט֣וֹב זֶ֔ה וְאֶל בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה טוֹבָ֖ה יָבֽוֹא

וַיֹּאמְרוּ֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶל רֵעֵ֜הוּ לֹֽא כֵ֣ן אֲנַ֣חְנוּ עֹשִׂ֗ים הַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ יוֹם בְּשֹׂרָ֣ה ה֔וּא וַאֲנַ֣חְנוּ מַחְשִׁ֗ים וְחִכִּ֛ינוּ עַד א֥וֹר הַבֹּ֖קֶר וּמְצָאָ֣נוּ עָו֑וֹן וְעַתָּה֙ לְכ֣וּ וְנָבֹ֔אָה וְנַגִּ֖ידָה בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּֽלֶךְ

title: dâth: a word shared by Esther and Moses
summary: דָּת (dâth, H1881) occurs in 21 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Esther (19) and Moses (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וַיֹּאמַ֗ר יְהוָ֞ה מִסִּינַ֥י בָּא֙ וְזָרַ֤ח מִשֵּׂעִיר֙ לָ֔מוֹ הוֹפִ֨יעַ֙ מֵהַ֣ר פָּארָ֔ן וְאָתָ֖ה מֵרִבְבֹ֣ת קֹ֑דֶשׁ מִֽימִינ֕וֹ אשדת אֵ֥שׁ דָּ֖ת לָֽמוֹ
וַֽיִּתְּנ֣וּ אֶת דָּתֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ לַאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וּפַחֲו֖וֹת עֵ֣בֶר הַנָּהָ֑ר וְנִשְּׂא֥וּ אֶת הָעָ֖ם וְאֶת בֵּֽית הָאֱלֹהִֽים
וְהַשְּׁתִיָּ֥ה כַדָּ֖ת אֵ֣ין אֹנֵ֑ס כִּי כֵ֣ן יִסַּ֣ד הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ עַ֚ל כָּל רַ֣ב בֵּית֔וֹ לַעֲשׂ֖וֹת כִּרְצ֥וֹן אִישׁ וָאִֽישׁ
וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לַחֲכָמִ֖ים יֹדְעֵ֣י הָֽעִתִּ֑ים כִּי כֵן֙ דְּבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִפְנֵ֕י כָּל יֹדְעֵ֖י דָּ֥ת וָדִֽין
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֗וֹב יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר מַלְכוּת֙ מִלְּפָנָ֔יו וְיִכָּתֵ֛ב בְּדָתֵ֥י פָֽרַס וּמָדַ֖י וְלֹ֣א יַעֲב֑וֹר אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא תָב֜וֹא וַשְׁתִּ֗י לִפְנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ וּמַלְכוּתָהּ֙ יִתֵּ֣ן הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִרְעוּתָ֖הּ הַטּוֹבָ֥ה מִמֶּֽנָּה

וַיְהִ֗י בְּהִשָּׁמַ֤ע דְּבַר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְדָת֔וֹ וּֽבְהִקָּבֵ֞ץ נְעָר֥וֹת רַבּ֛וֹת אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה אֶל יַ֣ד הֵגָ֑י וַתִּלָּקַ֤ח אֶסְתֵּר֙ אֶל בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֶל יַ֥ד הֵגַ֖י שֹׁמֵ֥ר הַנָּשִֽׁים

וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ נַעֲרָ֨ה וְנַעֲרָ֜ה לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֗וֹשׁ מִקֵּץ֩ הֱי֨וֹת לָ֜הּ כְּדָ֤ת הַנָּשִׁים֙ שְׁנֵ֣ים עָשָׂ֣ר חֹ֔דֶשׁ כִּ֛י כֵּ֥ן יִמְלְא֖וּ יְמֵ֣י מְרוּקֵיהֶ֑ן שִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בְּשֶׁ֣מֶן הַמֹּ֔ר וְשִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בַּבְּשָׂמִ֔ים וּבְתַמְרוּקֵ֖י הַנָּשִֽׁים

וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ יֶשְׁנ֣וֹ עַם אֶחָ֗ד מְפֻזָּ֤ר וּמְפֹרָד֙ בֵּ֣ין הָֽעַמִּ֔ים בְּכֹ֖ל מְדִינ֣וֹת מַלְכוּתֶ֑ךָ וְדָתֵיהֶ֞ם שֹׁנ֣וֹת מִכָּל עָ֗ם וְאֶת דָּתֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֵינָ֣ם עֹשִׂ֔ים וְלַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֵין שֹׁוֶ֖ה לְהַנִּיחָֽם
פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן הַכְּתָ֗ב לְהִנָּ֤תֵֽן דָּת֙ בְּכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֔ה גָּל֖וּי לְכָל הָֽעַמִּ֑ים לִהְי֥וֹת עֲתִדִ֖ים לַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה
הָֽרָצִ֞ים יָצְא֤וּ דְחוּפִים֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה
וּבְכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֗ה מְקוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֨ר דְּבַר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְדָתוֹ֙ מַגִּ֔יעַ אֵ֤בֶל גָּדוֹל֙ לַיְּהוּדִ֔ים וְצ֥וֹם וּבְכִ֖י וּמִסְפֵּ֑ד שַׂ֣ק וָאֵ֔פֶר יֻצַּ֖ע לָֽרַבִּֽים

וְאֶת פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן כְּתָֽב הַ֠דָּת אֲשֶׁר נִתַּ֨ן בְּשׁוּשָׁ֤ן לְהַשְׁמִידָם֙ נָ֣תַן ל֔וֹ לְהַרְא֥וֹת אֶת אֶסְתֵּ֖ר וּלְהַגִּ֣יד לָ֑הּ וּלְצַוּ֣וֹת עָלֶ֗יהָ לָב֨וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ לְהִֽתְחַנֶּן ל֛וֹ וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל עַמָּֽהּ

כָּל עַבְדֵ֣י הַמֶּ֡לֶךְ וְעַם מְדִינ֨וֹת הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ יֽוֹדְעִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּל אִ֣ישׁ וְאִשָּׁ֡ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָבֽוֹא אֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ֩ אֶל הֶחָצֵ֨ר הַפְּנִימִ֜ית אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא יִקָּרֵ֗א אַחַ֤ת דָּתוֹ֙ לְהָמִ֔ית לְ֠בַד מֵאֲשֶׁ֨ר יֽוֹשִׁיט ל֥וֹ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת שַׁרְבִ֥יט הַזָּהָ֖ב וְחָיָ֑ה וַאֲנִ֗י לֹ֤א נִקְרֵ֨אתי֙ לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ זֶ֖ה שְׁלוֹשִׁ֥ים יֽוֹם

לֵךְ֩ כְּנ֨וֹס אֶת כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֜ים הַֽנִּמְצְאִ֣ים בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן וְצ֣וּמוּ עָ֠לַי וְאַל תֹּאכְל֨וּ וְאַל תִּשְׁתּ֜וּ שְׁלֹ֤שֶׁת יָמִים֙ לַ֣יְלָה וָי֔וֹם גַּם אֲנִ֥י וְנַעֲרֹתַ֖י אָצ֣וּם כֵּ֑ן וּבְכֵ֞ן אָב֤וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא כַדָּ֔ת וְכַאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָבַ֖דְתִּי אָבָֽדְתִּי

title: malkâh: a word shared by Esther and Solomon
summary: מַלְכָּה (malkâh, H4436) occurs in 34 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Esther (24) and Solomon (8). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שֹׁמַ֛עַת אֶת שֵׁ֥מַע שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה לְשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה וַתָּבֹ֥א לְנַסֹּת֖וֹ בְּחִידֽוֹת
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת כָּל חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה

וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים הַרְבֵּ֥ה מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה לֹא בָא֩ כַבֹּ֨שֶׂם הַה֥וּא עוֹד֙ לָרֹ֔ב אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַד֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָֽתַן לָ֔הּ כְּיַ֖ד הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וַתֵּ֛פֶן וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ

וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שָֽׁמְעָה֮ אֶת שֵׁ֣מַע שְׁלֹמֹה֒ וַתָּב֣וֹא לְנַסּוֹת֩ אֶת שְׁלֹמֹ֨ה בְחִיד֜וֹת בִּירֽוּשָׁלִַ֗ם בְּחַ֣יִל כָּבֵ֣ד מְאֹ֡ד וּ֠גְמַלִּים נֹשְׂאִ֨ים בְּשָׂמִ֧ים וְזָהָ֛ב לָרֹ֖ב וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וַתָּבוֹא֙ אֶל שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה וַתְּדַבֵּ֣ר עִמּ֔וֹ אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָיָ֖ה עִם לְבָבָֽהּ
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה
וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים לָרֹ֥ב מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וְלֹ֤א הָיָה֙ כַּבֹּ֣שֶׂם הַה֔וּא אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַ֖ד אֲשֶׁר הֵבִ֣יאָה אֶל הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַֽתַּהֲפֹ֛ךְ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ
גַּ֚ם וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה עָשְׂתָ֖ה מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה נָשִׁ֑ים בֵּ֚ית הַמַּלְכ֔וּת אֲשֶׁ֖ר לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
לְ֠הָבִיא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּכֶ֣תֶר מַלְכ֑וּת לְהַרְא֨וֹת הָֽעַמִּ֤ים וְהַשָּׂרִים֙ אֶת יָפְיָ֔הּ כִּֽי טוֹבַ֥ת מַרְאֶ֖ה הִֽיא
וַתְּמָאֵ֞ן הַמַּלְכָּ֣ה וַשְׁתִּ֗י לָבוֹא֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּיַ֣ד הַסָּרִיסִ֑ים וַיִּקְצֹ֤ף הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מְאֹ֔ד וַחֲמָת֖וֹ בָּעֲרָ֥ה בֽוֹ
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מומכן מְמוּכָ֗ן לִפְנֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְהַשָּׂרִ֔ים לֹ֤א עַל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְבַדּ֔וֹ עָוְתָ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֑ה כִּ֤י עַל כָּל הַשָּׂרִים֙ וְעַל כָּל הָ֣עַמִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֕ר בְּכָל מְדִינ֖וֹת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
כִּֽי יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר הַמַּלְכָּה֙ עַל כָּל הַנָּשִׁ֔ים לְהַבְז֥וֹת בַּעְלֵיהֶ֖ן בְּעֵינֵיהֶ֑ן בְּאָמְרָ֗ם הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֡וֹשׁ אָמַ֞ר לְהָבִ֨יא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לְפָנָ֖יו וְלֹא בָֽאָה
וְֽהַיּ֨וֹם הַזֶּ֜ה תֹּאמַ֣רְנָה שָׂר֣וֹת פָּֽרַס וּמָדַ֗י אֲשֶׁ֤ר שָֽׁמְעוּ֙ אֶת דְּבַ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה לְכֹ֖ל שָׂרֵ֣י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וּכְדַ֖י בִּזָּי֥וֹן וָקָֽצֶף

summary: מִלָּה (millâh, H4405) occurs in 38 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: David (1) and Job (34). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: ר֥וּחַ יְהוָ֖ה דִּבֶּר בִּ֑י וּמִלָּת֖וֹ עַל לְשׁוֹנִֽי
הֲנִסָּ֬ה דָבָ֣ר אֵלֶ֣יךָ תִּלְאֶ֑ה וַעְצֹ֥ר בְּ֝מִלִּ֗ין מִ֣י יוּכָֽל
כּ֭וֹשֵׁל יְקִימ֣וּן מִלֶּ֑יךָ וּבִרְכַּ֖יִם כֹּרְע֣וֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ
הַלְהוֹכַ֣ח מִלִּ֣ים תַּחְשֹׁ֑בוּ וּ֝לְר֗וּחַ אִמְרֵ֥י נֹאָֽשׁ
הֲלֹא הֵ֣ם י֭וֹרוּךָ יֹ֣אמְרוּ לָ֑ךְ וּ֝מִלִּבָּ֗ם יוֹצִ֥אוּ מִלִּֽים
הֲלֹא אֹ֭זֶן מִלִּ֣ין תִּבְחָ֑ן וְ֝חֵ֗ךְ אֹ֣כֶל יִטְעַם לֽוֹ
שִׁמְע֣וּ שָׁ֭מוֹעַ מִלָּתִ֑י וְ֝אַֽחֲוָתִ֗י בְּאָזְנֵיכֶֽם
הוֹכֵ֣חַ בְּ֭דָבָר לֹ֣א יִסְכּ֑וֹן וּ֝מִלִּ֗ים לֹא יוֹעִ֥יל בָּֽם

וַיַּ֥רְא שַׂר הָאֹפִ֖ים כִּ֣י ט֣וֹב פָּתָ֑ר וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל יוֹסֵ֔ף אַף אֲנִי֙ בַּחֲלוֹמִ֔י וְהִנֵּ֗ה שְׁלֹשָׁ֛ה סַלֵּ֥י חֹרִ֖י עַל רֹאשִֽׁי
וְאֵ֛ת שַׂ֥ר הָאֹפִ֖ים תָּלָ֑ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר פָּתַ֛ר לָהֶ֖ם יוֹסֵֽף
וַיְהִ֤י בַבֹּ֨קֶר֙ וַתִּפָּ֣עֶם רוּח֔וֹ וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח וַיִּקְרָ֛א אֶת כָּל חַרְטֻמֵּ֥י מִצְרַ֖יִם וְאֶת כָּל חֲכָמֶ֑יהָ וַיְסַפֵּ֨ר פַּרְעֹ֤ה לָהֶם֙ אֶת חֲלֹמ֔וֹ וְאֵין פּוֹתֵ֥ר אוֹתָ֖ם לְפַרְעֹֽה
וְשָׁ֨ם אִתָּ֜נוּ נַ֣עַר עִבְרִ֗י עֶ֚בֶד לְשַׂ֣ר הַטַּבָּחִ֔ים וַנְּ֨סַפֶּר ל֔וֹ וַיִּפְתָּר לָ֖נוּ אֶת חֲלֹמֹתֵ֑ינוּ אִ֥ישׁ כַּחֲלֹמ֖וֹ פָּתָֽר
וַיְהִ֛י כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר פָּֽתַר לָ֖נוּ כֵּ֣ן הָיָ֑ה אֹתִ֛י הֵשִׁ֥יב עַל כַּנִּ֖י וְאֹת֥וֹ תָלָֽה
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר פַּרְעֹה֙ אֶל יוֹסֵ֔ף חֲל֣וֹם חָלַ֔מְתִּי וּפֹתֵ֖ר אֵ֣ין אֹת֑וֹ וַאֲנִ֗י שָׁמַ֤עְתִּי עָלֶ֨יךָ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר תִּשְׁמַ֥ע חֲל֖וֹם לִפְתֹּ֥ר אֹתֽוֹ

passages.text: אֶת הַמְּנֹרָ֨ה הַטְּהֹרָ֜ה אֶת נֵרֹתֶ֗יהָ נֵרֹ֛ת הַמַּֽעֲרָכָ֖ה וְאֶת כָּל כֵּלֶ֑יהָ וְאֵ֖ת שֶׁ֥מֶן הַמָּאֽוֹר
וְשַׂמְתָּ֥ אוֹתָ֛ם שְׁתַּ֥יִם מַֽעֲרָכ֖וֹת שֵׁ֣שׁ הַֽמַּעֲרָ֑כֶת עַ֛ל הַשֻּׁלְחָ֥ן הַטָּהֹ֖ר לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה
וּבָנִ֨יתָ מִזְבֵּ֜חַ לַיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ עַ֣ל רֹ֧אשׁ הַמָּע֛וֹז הַזֶּ֖ה בַּמַּֽעֲרָכָ֑ה וְלָֽקַחְתָּ֙ אֶת הַפָּ֣ר הַשֵּׁנִ֔י וְהַעֲלִ֣יתָ עוֹלָ֔ה בַּעֲצֵ֥י הָאֲשֵׁרָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּכְרֹֽת
וַיַּעַרְכ֨וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֜ים לִקְרַ֣את יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַתִּטֹּשׁ֙ הַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וַיִּנָּ֥גֶף יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיַּכּ֤וּ בַמַּֽעֲרָכָה֙ בַּשָּׂדֶ֔ה כְּאַרְבַּ֥עַת אֲלָפִ֖ים אִֽישׁ
וַיָּ֤רָץ אִישׁ בִּנְיָמִן֙ מֵהַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וַיָּבֹ֥א שִׁלֹ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וּמַדָּ֣יו קְרֻעִ֔ים וַאֲדָמָ֖ה עַל רֹאשֽׁוֹ
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הָאִ֜ישׁ אֶל עֵלִ֗י אָֽנֹכִי֙ הַבָּ֣א מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֔ה וַאֲנִ֕י מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֖ה נַ֣סְתִּי הַיּ֑וֹם וַיֹּ֛אמֶר מֶֽה הָיָ֥ה הַדָּבָ֖ר בְּנִֽי

וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֗ד וַיִּקְרָא֙ אֶל מַעַרְכֹ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם לָ֥מָּה תֵצְא֖וּ לַעֲרֹ֣ךְ מִלְחָמָ֑ה הֲל֧וֹא אָנֹכִ֣י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֗י וְאַתֶּם֙ עֲבָדִ֣ים לְשָׁא֔וּל בְּרוּ לָכֶ֥ם אִ֖ישׁ וְיֵרֵ֥ד אֵלָֽי
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אֲנִ֗י חֵרַ֛פְתִּי אֶת מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה תְּנוּ לִ֣י אִ֔ישׁ וְנִֽלָּחֲמָ֖ה יָֽחַד

וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם דָּוִ֜ד בַּבֹּ֗קֶר וַיִּטֹּ֤שׁ אֶת הַצֹּאן֙ עַל שֹׁמֵ֔ר וַיִּשָּׂ֣א וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר צִוָּ֖הוּ יִשָׁ֑י וַיָּבֹא֙ הַמַּעְגָּ֔לָה וְהַחַ֗יִל הַיֹּצֵא֙ אֶל הַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וְהֵרֵ֖עוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה
וַתַּעֲרֹ֤ךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים מַעֲרָכָ֖ה לִקְרַ֥את מַעֲרָכָֽה
וַיִּטֹּשׁ֩ דָּוִ֨ד אֶת הַכֵּלִ֜ים מֵעָלָ֗יו עַל יַד֙ שׁוֹמֵ֣ר הַכֵּלִ֔ים וַיָּ֖רָץ הַמַּעֲרָכָ֑ה וַיָּבֹ֕א וַיִּשְׁאַ֥ל לְאֶחָ֖יו לְשָׁלֽוֹם
וְה֣וּא מְדַבֵּ֣ר עִמָּ֗ם וְהִנֵּ֣ה אִ֣ישׁ הַבֵּנַ֡יִם עוֹלֶ֞ה גָּלְיָת֩ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י שְׁמ֤וֹ מִגַּת֙ ממערות מִמַּעַרְכ֣וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַיְדַבֵּ֖ר כַּדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּשְׁמַ֖ע דָּוִֽד

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗ד אֶֽל הָאֲנָשִׁ֞ים הָעֹמְדִ֣ים עִמּוֹ֮ לֵאמֹר֒ מַה יֵּעָשֶׂ֗ה לָאִישׁ֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר יַכֶּה֙ אֶת הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֣י הַלָּ֔ז וְהֵסִ֥יר חֶרְפָּ֖ה מֵעַ֣ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י מִ֗י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֤י הֶֽעָרֵל֙ הַזֶּ֔ה כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכ֖וֹת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
גַּ֧ם אֶֽת הָאֲרִ֛י גַּם הַדּ֖וֹב הִכָּ֣ה עַבְדֶּ֑ךָ וְֽ֠הָיָה הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י הֶעָרֵ֤ל הַזֶּה֙ כְּאַחַ֣ד מֵהֶ֔ם כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכֹ֖ת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אַתָּה֙ בָּ֣א אֵלַ֔י בְּחֶ֖רֶב וּבַחֲנִ֣ית וּבְכִיד֑וֹן וְאָנֹכִ֣י בָֽא אֵלֶ֗יךָ בְּשֵׁם֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֛י מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר חֵרַֽפְתָּ

title: Satan refuses to bow to Adam
summary: God commands the angels to honor Adam, and Satan refuses. Found in the Life of Adam and Eve and the Cave of Treasures, and repeatedly in the Quran.

passages.ref: Life of Adam and Eve (Latin Vita 12–16)

title: The Kalam cosmological argument
summary: The argument that the universe began and so has a cause, developed by the mutakallimūn and al-Ghazali, was revived and named by William Lane Craig in analytic philosophy of religion.

passages.ref: W. L. Craig, The Kalām Cosmological Argument (1979)

title: Panchatantra to Kalila wa-Dimna
summary: The Sanskrit Panchatantra was translated into Middle Persian (Burzoy, 6th c.), then Arabic (Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, 8th c.), then into Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and most European languages.

title: Kumarbi cycle and Hesiod's Theogony
summary: Both have the same succession myth: Anu, Kumarbi, Teshub in the Hurro-Hittite cycle and Ouranos, Kronos, Zeus in Hesiod, including a sky god castrated by his successor.

title: kursī: Sumerian throne to Quranic seat
summary: Sumerian guza passed into Akkadian kussû, Aramaic kursēʾ, and Arabic kursī. The Quran's Throne Verse (2:255) uses it.

passages.note: His kursī encompasses the heavens and the earth
passages.text: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِۦ يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَىْءٍ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَ وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفْظُهُمَا وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ

title: Mani and the 'seal of the prophets'
summary: Quran 33:40 calls Muhammad khātam al-nabiyyīn. Manichaean sources present Mani as the last in a line of prophets (Buddha, Zoroaster, Jesus), and whether 'seal' was a Manichaean title is debated.

title: Mary raised in the Temple
summary: The Protevangelium of James has Mary dedicated to the Temple, fed by an angel, and her guardian chosen by a sign. The Quran has Mary's dedication, miraculous provision in the sanctuary, Zechariah as guardian, and lots cast for her care.

passages.text: (3:35) إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱمْرَأَتُ عِمْرَٰنَ رَبِّ إِنِّى نَذَرْتُ لَكَ مَا فِى بَطْنِى مُحَرَّرًا فَتَقَبَّلْ مِنِّىٓ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ (3:36) فَلَمَّا وَضَعَتْهَا قَالَتْ رَبِّ إِنِّى وَضَعْتُهَآ أُنثَىٰ وَٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا وَضَعَتْ وَلَيْسَ ٱلذَّكَرُ كَٱلْأُنثَىٰ وَإِنِّى سَمَّيْتُهَا مَرْيَمَ وَإِنِّىٓ أُعِيذُهَا بِكَ وَذُرِّيَّتَهَا مِنَ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ (3:37) فَتَقَبَّلَهَا رَبُّهَا بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ وَأَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا زَكَرِيَّا ٱلْمِحْرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقًا قَالَ يَٰمَرْيَمُ أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا قَالَتْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشَآءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ (3:44) ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ أَنۢبَآءِ ٱلْغَيْبِ نُوحِيهِ إِلَيْكَ وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ يُلْقُونَ أَقْلَٰمَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ

title: Mary and the palm tree
summary: In Pseudo-Matthew a palm bends to feed Mary and a spring opens during the flight to Egypt. In the Quran a palm and a stream sustain Mary during the birth of Jesus.

Ahab says 'troubler' (ʿōkhēr), Thamūd use bird-augury language (iṭṭayyara, 'to take an ill omen'); Elijah blames their apostasy, Ṣāliḥ says their omen is with God.
Shared motifs, rarest first: King calls the prophet 'troubler of Israel' (okher Yisra'el); prophet returns the charge (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Contest on Mount Carmel: Prophet repairs the ruined altar with twelve stones for the tribes of Jacob; Contest of gods: the god who answers by fire on an unlit sacrifice is God; The prophets of Baal are seized and slaughtered at the brook Kishon; Prophets of Baal limp-dance around the altar and gash themselves with swords and lances till blood flows; Prophet mocks the silent god: perhaps he is musing, relieving himself, travelling, or asleep and must be woken; Sacrifice and altar drenched with four jars of water three times, filling a trench, before the miracle; The people fall on their faces crying 'YHWH, he is God! YHWH, he is God!'; How a public contest between God's prophet and the king's religious specialists ends [contrast between the texts]; An offering consumed by fire as proof of the true God or messenger [response between the texts]; Fire from heaven falls and consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust and water; 'How long will you hop between two branches? If YHWH is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him'; A single prophet of YHWH stands against 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah; and 10 more.

Only in Salih, the evil omen and the nine plotters of Thamud: The people say they augur ill (iṭṭayyarnā) of the prophet; he answers that their omen (ṭāʾir) is with God; The men of the prophet's hometown seek his life: 'Do not prophesy in YHWH's name or you will die by our hand'; Nine men of the city swear by God to attack the prophet and his family by night and deny it to his avenger; The prophet Ṣāliḥ is sent to the people of Thamūd; They plot a plot, and God plots a plot; give the deniers respite a little; Formula: 'their brother' (akhūhum) Noah/Hud/Salih/Lot is a trustworthy messenger sent to his people; The listeners walk among the dwellings of generations God destroyed, a sign.

title: Contest on Mount Carmel ↔ Misers, those who called God poor, and the fire-consumed offering
summary: These two units share 2 motifs: an offering consumed by fire as proof of the true god or messenger [response between the texts], fire from heaven falls and consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust and water.

passages.note: An offering consumed by fire as proof of the true God or messenger [response between the texts] (1Kgs 18:24, 38 wĕ-hāyâ hā-ʾĕlōhîm ʾăšer yaʿăneh bā-ʾēš hûʾ hā-ʾĕlōhîm ... wa-ttippōl ʾēš YHWH wa-ttōʾkal ʾet hā-ʿōlâ: the god who answers by fire is God, and the fire eats the offering; Q 3:183 qālū inna llāha ʿahida ilaynā allā nuʾmina li-rasūlin ḥattā yaʾtiyanā bi-qurbānin taʾkuluhu n-nāru qul qad jāʾakum rusulun min qablī bi-l-bayyināti wa-bi-lladhī qultum fa-li-ma qataltumūhum: they claim God made them promise to believe no messenger without an offering 'the fire eats' (ʾākal / akala); answer: messengers did bring it, so why did you kill them? The Carmel test is turned into the opponents' demand, and the demand is refuted from their own history.)

title: Contest on Mount Carmel ↔ The people of the town, the three messengers and the man who came running
summary: These two units share 1 motifs: the townsfolk say 'we augur ill of you' and threaten to stone the messengers; they reply 'your omen is with you'.

passages.note: The townsfolk say 'we augur ill of you' and threaten to stone the messengers; they reply 'your omen is with you' (The prophet blamed for the people's misfortune throws the charge back. ha-ʾattâ zeh ʿōḵēr yiśrāʾēl / lōʾ ʿāḵartî ʾeṯ-yiśrāʾēl kî ʾim-ʾattâ û-ḇêṯ ʾāḇîḵā ba-ʿăzāḇəḵem ʾeṯ-miṣwōṯ YHWH vs. innā taṭayyarnā bikum / ṭāʾirukum maʿakum ... bal antum qawmun musrifūn. 'Troubler' (ʿōḵēr) corresponds to the omen-bird (ṭāʾir); in both the bad luck is in the accusers' own sin.)

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/02-hb-quran.yaml): parallel. Q: mudhabdhabīna bayna dhālika lā ilā hāʾulāʾi wa-lā ilā hāʾulāʾi (dangling between). 1Kgs: ʿad-mātay ʾattem pōsəḥîm ʿal-štê ha-səʿippîm. Elijah demands a choice (ʾim-YHWH hā-ʾĕlōhîm ləkhû ʾaḥărāyw wə-ʾim-ha-baʿal ləkhû ʾaḥărāyw); Q describes hypocrites who belong to neither camp.
Shared motifs, rarest first: 'How long will you hop between two branches? If YHWH is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him' (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Contest on Mount Carmel: Prophet repairs the ruined altar with twelve stones for the tribes of Jacob; Contest of gods: the god who answers by fire on an unlit sacrifice is God; The prophets of Baal are seized and slaughtered at the brook Kishon; Prophets of Baal limp-dance around the altar and gash themselves with swords and lances till blood flows; Prophet mocks the silent god: perhaps he is musing, relieving himself, travelling, or asleep and must be woken; Sacrifice and altar drenched with four jars of water three times, filling a trench, before the miracle; The people fall on their faces crying 'YHWH, he is God! YHWH, he is God!'; How a public contest between God's prophet and the king's religious specialists ends [contrast between the texts]; An offering consumed by fire as proof of the true God or messenger [response between the texts]; Fire from heaven falls and consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust and water; A single prophet of YHWH stands against 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah; How the people respond to the prophet's challenge over Baal [divergence between the texts]; and 10 more.

Only in Articles of faith; hypocrites wavering between two sides: Belief in God, his angels, his books, his messengers and the last day; Those who believe in some messengers and reject others, making distinctions among them; God does not love public evil speech except by one who has been wronged; The hypocrites are in the lowest depth (al-dark al-asfal) of the fire; Those who believe, then disbelieve, then believe, then disbelieve and increase in disbelief; Good works (spending, prayer) done to be seen by people (riyāʾ); Do not take Jews and Christians (or mockers of your religion) as allies; Do not sit with those who plunge into mockery of God's signs until they change the subject; The hypocrites try to deceive God, but it is he who deceives them; God is near in their mouths but far from their kidneys (hearts); This people honors God with lips while its heart is far; its fear of him is a commandment of men learned by rote.

passages.text: وَلَا تَتَمَنَّوْا۟ مَا فَضَّلَ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍ لِّلرِّجَالِ نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا ٱكْتَسَبُوا۟ وَلِلنِّسَآءِ نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا ٱكْتَسَبْنَ وَسْـَٔلُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ مِن فَضْلِهِۦٓ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمًا

passages.note: Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness
passages.text: וְ֠הוֹשִׁיבוּ שְׁנַ֨יִם אֲנָשִׁ֥ים בְּנֵֽי בְלִיַּעַל֮ נֶגְדּוֹ֒ וִיעִדֻ֣הוּ לֵאמֹ֔ר בֵּרַ֥כְתָּ אֱלֹהִ֖ים וָמֶ֑לֶךְ וְהוֹצִיאֻ֥הוּ וְסִקְלֻ֖הוּ וְיָמֹֽת

passages.note: Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness
passages.text: וַ֠יָּבֹאוּ שְׁנֵ֨י הָאֲנָשִׁ֥ים בְּנֵֽי בְלִיַּעַל֮ וַיֵּשְׁב֣וּ נֶגְדּוֹ֒ וַיְעִדֻהוּ֩ אַנְשֵׁ֨י הַבְּלִיַּ֜עַל אֶת נָב֗וֹת נֶ֤גֶד הָעָם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר בֵּרַ֥ךְ נָב֛וֹת אֱלֹהִ֖ים וָמֶ֑לֶךְ וַיֹּצִאֻ֨הוּ֙ מִח֣וּץ לָעִ֔יר וַיִּסְקְלֻ֥הוּ בָאֲבָנִ֖ים וַיָּמֹֽת

passages.note: Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness (Exod 20:13, 15 lōʾ tirṣāḥ ... lōʾ tignōb; Q 4:29 lā taʾkulū amwālakum baynakum bi-l-bāṭili illā an takūna tijāratan ʿan tarāḍin minkum wa-lā taqtulū anfusakum: no wrongful taking of wealth (except by consented trade) and no killing, side by side as in the Decalogue.)
passages.text: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تَأْكُلُوٓا۟ أَمْوَٰلَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ إِلَّآ أَن تَكُونَ تِجَٰرَةً عَن تَرَاضٍ مِّنكُمْ وَلَا تَقْتُلُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِكُمْ رَحِيمًا

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Prohibition of coveting the neighbor's wife and property (weight 5.8); Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness (weight 5.1). Pair score 10.9.

Only in Naboth's vineyard: Commoner refuses to sell or trade his ancestral vineyard to the king: 'God forbid I give you my fathers' inheritance'; Thwarted king lies on his bed, turns his face to the wall and refuses to eat; Queen writes letters in the king's name, sealed with his seal, ordering a judicial murder; A fast is proclaimed and two worthless men falsely testify that the victim 'blessed (cursed) God and king'; Innocent victim is taken outside the city and stoned to death; King goes home 'sullen and angry' (sar ve-za'ef) after a prophet's rebuke; Offender stoned to death by the community.

Only in Wealth by consent, major sins, and discord in marriage: Command: do not kill yourselves (or one another); In marital discord an arbiter is sent from his family and one from hers; If the major sins (kabāʾir) are avoided, God expiates lesser misdeeds; Men are maintainers (qawwāmūn) of women by God's preference and their spending; A wife whose rebellion (nushūz) is feared is admonished, left alone in bed, then struck; Those bound to you by oath-alliance receive their share; Prohibition of coveting the neighbor's wife and property [divergence between the texts]; The ground of a husband's authority over his wife [divergence between the texts]; Do not consume one another's wealth wrongfully (bil-bāṭil), only by trade with mutual consent.
Naboth's vineyard: tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hebrew.
Wealth by consent, major sins, and discord in marriage: tagged by Claude (model), reading the Arabic.

title: Micaiah son of Imlah and the lying spirit ↔ Micaiah ben Imlah, the lying spirit in the divine council, and Ahab's death
summary: These two units share 7 motifs: a spirit volunteers in the divine council to be a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths, court prophet makes iron horns: 'with these you will gore aram', four hundred court prophets unanimously promise victory, a false prophet strikes the true prophet on the cheek….

passages.note: A spirit volunteers in the divine council to be a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths
passages.text: (22:22) וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֵצֵא֙ וְהָיִ֨יתִי֙ ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּפִ֖י כָּל נְבִיאָ֑יו וַיֹּ֗אמֶר תְּפַתֶּה֙ וְגַם תּוּכָ֔ל צֵ֖א וַעֲשֵׂה כֵֽן (22:23) וְעַתָּ֗ה הִנֵּ֨ה נָתַ֤ן יְהוָה֙ ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּפִ֖י כָּל נְבִיאֶ֣יךָ אֵ֑לֶּה וַֽיהוָ֔ה דִּבֶּ֥ר עָלֶ֖יךָ רָעָֽה

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A round vessel ten cubits across measures thirty around (pi taken as three) (weight 6.7); Bronze vessels cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan (weight 6.7); The bronze used for the sanctuary is so abundant its weight was not determined (weight 6.7); An accounting of the gold, silver and bronze used for the sanctuary (weight 6.3); A gold table with the bread of the presence always before God (weight 6.0); A great cast-bronze 'sea' basin rests on twelve bronze oxen facing the four directions in threes (weight 6.0). Pair score 38.4.

Only in The bronze sea, wheeled stands and temple vessels: Ten golden lampstands stand before the inner sanctuary, five on each side; Ten wheeled bronze stands decorated with lions, oxen, cherubim and palms carry basins; How Solomon's great bronze works were produced [divergence between the texts]; Exact dimensions in cubits are given for a sacred object of the sanctuary; A bronze laver where priests wash hands and feet before service, lest they die; A small gold-plated altar for burning incense before the veil.

Only in Bronze altar, the molten sea on twelve oxen, lavers, lampstands and tables: A great bronze altar twenty cubits square and ten high; The temple has a court of the priests and a great court; The rim of the bronze sea is shaped like a lily blossom; The bronze sea serves for the priests to wash in, the lavers for rinsing offerings; Ten gold lampstands and ten tables, five on each side; Two named bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz, before the temple.

title: The bronze sea, wheeled stands and temple vessels ↔ David's mountains and mail; Solomon's wind, copper, jinn and staff
summary: These two units share 2 motifs: how solomon's great bronze works were produced [divergence between the texts], a great cast-bronze 'sea' basin rests on twelve bronze oxen facing the four directions in threes.

passages.note: How Solomon's great bronze works were produced [divergence between the texts] (Solomon's cast bronze. 1 Kgs: wa-yyaʿaś ʾeṯ-ha-yyām mûṣāq ... ʿōmēḏ ʿal-šənê ʿāśār bāqār; bə-kikkar ha-yyardēn yəṣāqām ha-mmeleḵ bə-maʿăḇēh hā-ʾăḏāmâ (cast in clay moulds in the Jordan plain). Q: wa-asalnā lahu ʿayna l-qiṭr (God makes a spring of molten copper flow for him) ... wa-jifānin ka-l-jawābi wa-qudūrin rāsiyāt. The metal comes from a miraculous spring instead of the foundry, and the 'sea' and its stands are matched by basins like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons. Lead: identification of the jifān/qudūr with the yām and mekonot is a proposal.)

Solomon's cast bronze. 1 Kgs: wa-yyaʿaś ʾeṯ-ha-yyām mûṣāq ... ʿōmēḏ ʿal-šənê ʿāśār bāqār; bə-kikkar ha-yyardēn yəṣāqām ha-mmeleḵ bə-maʿăḇēh hā-ʾăḏāmâ (cast in clay moulds in the Jordan plain). Q: wa-asalnā lahu ʿayna l-qiṭr (God makes a spring of molten copper flow for him) ... wa-jifānin ka-l-jawābi wa-qudūrin rāsiyāt. The metal comes from a miraculous spring instead of the foundry, and the 'sea' and its stands are matched by basins like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons. evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A foreigner from a far land who hears of God's name comes to pray at the temple and is heard (weight 6.7); 'There is no man who does not sin' (weight 6.7); Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, much less a temple (weight 6.3); The direction faced in prayer [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Prayers made toward the temple (or toward the land, city and house when in exile) are heard in heaven (weight 6.0); Prophet spreads out his palms to God in prayer (weight 5.4); Heaven and the heaven of heavens belong to God (weight 5.4). Pair score 42.5.

Only in Solomon's prayer of dedication: Exiles in an enemy land turn back with all their heart and pray toward their land, and God grants them mercy before captors; A man accused swears a curse-oath before the altar, and God judges guilty and innocent; Long catalogue of curses for covenant violation (disease, defeat, famine, exile); Egypt called an iron furnace (smelting furnace); Heaven is shut and no rain falls because of the people's sin; repentance brings rain; God alone knows the hearts of all humans.

Only in Solomon's blessing and dedication prayer on the bronze platform: Prayer lists famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, siege and sickness as occasions for prayer; The king kneels on a bronze platform in the court and spreads his hands to heaven; An oath sworn before God's altar in the temple, judged by God; People away from Jerusalem or in exile pray in the direction of the land, city and temple; Captives confess in exile 'We have sinned, done wrong and acted wickedly'; 'Arise, YHWH, to your resting place, you and the ark of your might'; Temple called a 'house of zebul' (exalted dwelling), a place for God to dwell forever; 'O my servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of God's mercy; God forgives all sins'; God has said he will dwell in thick darkness ('arafel); The dynasty's continuance is conditioned on the heirs' faithfulness; God looks on the heart, not on appearance or height; Sacrifice only at the place God will choose to make his name dwell; and 1 more.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. jiʾtuka min Sabaʾin bi-nabaʾin yaqīnin innī wajadtu mraʾatan tamlikuhum ~ û-malkat Šəvāʾ šāməʿâ ʾet šēmaʿ Šəlōmōh wat-tāvôʾ: a woman ruling Sheba (Sabaʾ / Šəvāʾ), a report (nabaʾ / šēmaʿ), and her coming to Solomon. The direction of the report is reversed: in Chronicles she hears of Solomon, in the Quran Solomon hears of her through the hoopoe. Who tests whom: in Chronicles the queen comes to test Solomon with riddles (lənassôt ʾet Šəlōmōh bə-ḥîdôt) and he answers all (wə-lōʾ neʿlam dāvār miš-Šəlōmōh); in the Quran Solomon tests the queen: nakkirū lahā ʿarshahā nanẓur a-tahtadī, and she answers ka-annahu huwa. The gifts: Chronicles has the queen bring 120 talents of gold, spices and gems, which Solomon accepts, and he gives her all she desires (nātan ... ʾet kol ḥefṣāh). In the Quran she sends a gift (hadiyya) to test him, and Solomon refuses it, a-tumiddūnani bi-mālin fa-mā ātāniya llāhu khayrun mimmā ātākum, and threatens to invade with armies they cannot resist. The queen overwhelmed by Solomon's building: Chronicles has her see the house he built (wə-hab-bayit ʾăšer bānâ) until wə-lōʾ hāyâ ʿôd bāh rûaḥ; the Quran has the palace of smooth glass (ṣarḥun mumarradun min qawārīr) that she takes for deep water (ḥasibathu lujjatan) and uncovers her legs. Awe becomes a test she fails and then learns from. cf. Targum Sheni Esther 1:2 (glass floor), outside the HB. The queen's last word: Chronicles has a blessing of Solomon's God, yəhî YHWH ʾĕlōhêkā bārûkh ʾăšer ḥāfēṣ bəkhā lə-tittəkhā ʿal kisʾô, 'your God', praised for Israel's king. The Quran has a conversion: rabbi innī ẓalamtu nafsī wa-aslamtu maʿa Sulaymāna lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn, after the hoopoe reported that she and her people worshipped the sun (27:24). Chronicles never calls her an idolater. The great throne: Chronicles praises Solomon's own (wa-yyaʿaś ham-melekh kissēʾ šēn gādôl wa-yṣappēhû zāhāv ṭāhôr); in the Quran the great throne is the queen's (wa-lahā ʿarshun ʿaẓīmun), and Solomon has it carried to him in the blink of an eye by one with knowledge of the Book.

Shared motifs, rarest first: The queen of Sheba visits Solomon (weight 6.7); The great throne in the Sheba story, and whose it is [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); Who tests whom between Solomon and the queen of Sheba [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); The queen of Sheba's gifts and Solomon's response [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); The queen of Sheba overwhelmed by Solomon's buildings [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); A foreign queen tests the king with riddles and he answers them all (weight 6.3); What the queen of Sheba says of Solomon's God [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3). Pair score 46.0.

Only in The Queen of Sheba tests Solomon; his gold, ivory throne, ships and death: A foreign ruler blesses Israel's God for setting the king on his throne; The king exceeds all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom; All the kings of Arabia and governors bring gold and silver; An annual income of 666 talents of gold; A visitor says she did not believe the report until she saw: not half was told her; Rare almug wood from Ophir used for temple supports and lyres for singers; never seen again; Promised land stretches from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates; A visitor seeing the king's court is left breathless ('no more spirit in her'); A royal visitor arrives with camels carrying spices, gold and precious stones; Great ivory throne overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lions on the steps and two beside the arms; Tarshish ships every three years bring gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks (or baboons); Shields of beaten gold made or captured and displayed; and 6 more.

Only in Solomon, the speech of birds, the ants, the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba: Entering Solomon's palace, the queen takes its floor of smooth glass for a pool and bares her legs; The hoopoe returns with sure news from Sabaʾ, knowledge Solomon lacked; Solomon sends the hoopoe to drop his letter before the queen and wait for their reply; Solomon reviews the birds, finds the hoopoe absent and threatens to punish or slaughter it unless it brings a clear excuse; An ʿifrīt of the jinn offers to bring the queen's throne before Solomon rises from his seat; Solomon's letter begins 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' and demands submission; The queen sends a gift to see what the envoys bring back; Solomon rejects the wealth and threatens invasion; The queen confesses she wronged herself and submits with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds; Solomon has the queen's throne disguised to test whether she recognizes it; she says 'It is as though it were it'; The queen and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God; Solomon inherits from David (knowledge and kingship); Solomon prays to be inspired to thank God for favor to him and his parents and to be admitted among the righteous; and 16 more.

title: Athaliah's usurpation and the hidden prince Joash ↔ Jehoiada's coup with the Levites; Joash crowned, Athaliah killed, Baal temple destroyed
summary: These two units share 5 motifs: king david's spears and shields kept in the temple are issued to the guards, a priest organizes the guards to overthrow a ruler and enthrone the hidden heir, coronation in which the king receives the crown (nezer) and the 'testimony' (edut), the temple of baal is torn down and its priest slain before the altars….

title: The resettled peoples, the lions and the syncretistic cult of Samaria ↔ Pagan portions and taboos; eight pairs; what is forbidden to all and to the Jews
summary: These two units share 2 motifs: settlers fear yhwh yet serve their own gods (syncretism), nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods.

passages.note: Settlers fear YHWH yet serve their own gods (syncretism)
passages.text: וַיִּהְי֥וּ יְרֵאִ֖ים אֶת יְהוָ֑ה וַיַּעֲשׂ֨וּ לָהֶ֤ם מִקְצוֹתָם֙ כֹּהֲנֵ֣י בָמ֔וֹת וַיִּהְי֛וּ עֹשִׂ֥ים לָהֶ֖ם בְּבֵ֥ית הַבָּמֽוֹת

passages.note: Settlers fear YHWH yet serve their own gods (syncretism)
passages.text: אֶת יְהוָ֖ה הָי֣וּ יְרֵאִ֑ים וְאֶת אֱלֹֽהֵיהֶם֙ הָי֣וּ עֹֽבְדִ֔ים כְּמִשְׁפַּט֙ הַגּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁר הִגְל֥וּ אֹתָ֖ם מִשָּֽׁם

Q: wa-jaʿalū li-llāhi mimmā dharaʾa mina l-ḥarthi wa-l-anʿāmi naṣīban fa-qālū hādhā li-llāhi ... wa-hādhā li-shurakāʾinā. Q adds that God's share ends up going to the partners.)
passages.text: وَجَعَلُوا۟ لِلَّهِ مِمَّا ذَرَأَ مِنَ ٱلْحَرْثِ وَٱلْأَنْعَٰمِ نَصِيبًا فَقَالُوا۟ هَٰذَا لِلَّهِ بِزَعْمِهِمْ وَهَٰذَا لِشُرَكَآئِنَا فَمَا كَانَ لِشُرَكَآئِهِمْ فَلَا يَصِلُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَمَا كَانَ لِلَّهِ فَهُوَ يَصِلُ إِلَىٰ شُرَكَآئِهِمْ سَآءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ

passages.text: قَدْ خَسِرَ ٱلَّذِينَ قَتَلُوٓا۟ أَوْلَٰدَهُمْ سَفَهًۢا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ وَحَرَّمُوا۟ مَا رَزَقَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ ٱفْتِرَآءً عَلَى ٱللَّهِ قَدْ ضَلُّوا۟ وَمَا كَانُوا۟ مُهْتَدِينَ

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/02-hb-quran.yaml): parallel. Dividing worship between God and other gods. 2Kgs: ʾet-YHWH hāyû yərēʾîm wə-ʾet-ʾĕlōhêhem hāyû ʿōvədîm. Q: wa-jaʿalū li-llāhi mimmā dharaʾa mina l-ḥarthi wa-l-anʿāmi naṣīban fa-qālū hādhā li-llāhi ... wa-hādhā li-shurakāʾinā. Q adds that God's share ends up going to the partners.
Shared motifs, rarest first: Settlers fear YHWH yet serve their own gods (syncretism) (weight 6.7); Nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods (weight 5.2). Pair score 11.9.

Only in The resettled peoples, the lions and the syncretistic cult of Samaria: Catalogue of foreign gods brought by settler peoples (Succoth-benoth, Nergal, Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, Adrammelech, Anammelech); Each land has a god whose 'manner' (mishpat) newcomers must learn; God sends lions to kill settlers who do not know the 'law of the god of the land'; Empire settles foreign peoples in the cities of a deported population; A deported priest is sent back to teach the settlers how to fear the local god; Mutual declaration: Israel avows YHWH as God, YHWH avows Israel as his treasured people.

Only in Pagan portions and taboos; eight pairs; what is forbidden to all and to the Jews: Pagans set apart cattle whose backs may not be ridden or burdened; Eight in pairs: sheep, goats, camels and cattle, male and female; which did God forbid?; Idolaters say 'had God willed we would not have associated partners nor forbidden anything'; Give its due on the day of harvest; For the Jews God forbade every animal with claws/undivided hoof and the fat of cattle and sheep except on backs, entrails or bone; Do not be wasteful; God does not love the wasteful (musrifīn); Pagans assign a portion of crops and cattle to God and a portion to their partners; Pagans declare certain cattle and crops taboo (ḥijr), to be eaten only by whom they will; Pagans reserve what is in the wombs of cattle for males, forbidden to wives unless stillborn; The camel is unclean because it does not have a split hoof [contrast between the texts]; List of clean and unclean animals: split hoof and chewing cud [response between the texts]; The fat tail of the sheep is offered [divergence between the texts]; and 11 more.

title: Hezekiah's reform; Sennacherib's invasion and the Rabshakeh's speech ↔ Sennacherib's invasion; the Rabshakeh's speech at the conduit

evidence.text: Passages are shown for the 10 rarest of 12 shared motifs; the full list follows.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Each man under his own vine and fig tree, drinking from his own cistern (weight 6.7); Invader promises deportees a land like their own, of grain, wine, oil and honey (weight 6.7); Officials ask the envoy to speak Aramaic, not Judean, so the people on the wall will not understand (weight 6.7); Invader claims the defenders' own god sent him to destroy the land (weight 6.7); The people keep silent and do not answer the enemy at the king's command (weight 6.7); Enemy envoy addresses the besieged at the city wall to break their morale (weight 6.7); Egypt likened to a broken reed staff that pierces the hand of whoever leans on it (weight 6.3); Threat that the besieged will eat their own dung and drink their urine (weight 6.3); Taunt: Where are the gods of the conquered nations? Could they save their lands from my hand? (weight 5.8); An Assyrian king named in the narrative (Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon) (weight 5.6); Command to smash altars, standing stones and Asherah poles and burn idols (weight 5.3); Men tear their garments in grief or dismay (weight 4.9). Pair score 74.3.

Only in Hezekiah's reform; Sennacherib's invasion and the Rabshakeh's speech: King smashes the bronze serpent made by Moses, called Nehushtan, because people burned incense to it; Image of a serpent on a pole heals those who look at it; Formula: there was none like him among all the kings before or after; A capital city is besieged for three years before it falls; King strips the temple and palace treasuries to buy off an invader; Conquered population deported to Assyria or another distant land.

Only in Sennacherib's invasion; the Rabshakeh's speech at the conduit: Prophet meets the king at the conduit of the upper pool on the highway of the Fuller's Field; Judah (or allies) put trust in Egypt and Cush for help against Assyria and are put to shame.

evidence.text: Passages are shown for the 10 rarest of 19 shared motifs; the full list follows.

Shared motifs, rarest first: The escaped remnant shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward; a remnant goes out from Zion (weight 6.7); The king tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and goes into the temple in crisis (weight 6.7); King spreads the enemy's threatening letter before God in the temple (weight 6.7); The enemy is said to reproach (harref) 'the living God' (weight 6.7); Sign: this year eat aftergrowth, next year what springs of itself, the third year sow and reap (weight 6.7); God puts a spirit in the invader so that he hears a rumor and returns home (weight 6.7); The arrogant king boasts of climbing the heights of Lebanon and cutting its cedars, drying up rivers with his feet (weight 6.7); The 'virgin daughter of Zion' laughs at and wags her head after the enemy (weight 6.7); The angel of YHWH strikes 185,000 in the enemy camp in one night; at dawn all are corpses (weight 6.7); Royal parricides flee to the land of Ararat (weight 6.7); Proverb of crisis: children have come to the birth-stool and there is no strength to deliver (weight 6.7); God says the conqueror's victories were planned by him long ago; the conqueror is only his instrument (weight 6.7); God's angels strike the enemy army [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); Enemy king is murdered by his own sons while worshipping in his god's temple (weight 6.3); God defends the city for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant (weight 6.0); Conquered nations' gods were burned because they were no gods, only wood and stone made by hands (weight 5.8); Taunt: Where are the gods of the conquered nations? Could they save their lands from my hand? (weight 5.8); God will put his hook in the enemy king's nose and his bit in his lips and lead him back (weight 5.8); God addressed as enthroned (yoshev) on the cherubim (weight 5.4). evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A cake of figs laid on a boil heals the king (weight 6.7); Given a choice of signs, the king picks the harder (shadow going backward) (weight 6.7); Prophet tells the sick king 'Set your house in order, for you shall die' (weight 6.7); Dying man turns his face to the wall and prays, weeping (weight 6.7); In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.3); In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life (weight 6.3); As a sign the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway (dial) of Ahaz (weight 6.3); At a leader's command the sun and moon stand still until the battle is won (weight 6.0). Pair score 51.6.

Only in Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps and the Babylonian envoys: The king proudly shows foreign envoys all his treasures, prompting a prophecy of their loss; A king receives a foreign ruler's envoys and gift [contrast between the texts]; King accepts doom for his descendants, glad there will be peace and truth in his own days; Prophecy that the king's descendants will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon; King makes a pool and conduit to bring water into the city; God defends the city for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant.

Only in Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps of Ahaz, and Hezekiah's psalm: Speaker laments that in the noon of his days he must go to the gates of Sheol, deprived of the rest of his years; A psalm-like 'writing' (mikhtav) of the king composed when he was sick and recovered; My dwelling is pulled up like a shepherd's tent; I have rolled up my life like a weaver, he cuts me off from the loom; In distress the sufferer chirps like a swift or crane and moans like a dove; God has cast all the speaker's sins behind his back and held back his soul from the pit of destruction; The dead cannot praise God: no wonders for the dead, no hesed in the grave, no faithfulness in Abaddon; A dying person's plea to God for more life, and God's answer [contrast between the texts]; On that day neither wealth nor sons avail, only one who comes to God with a sound heart; Bequest (wasiyya) to parents and kin prescribed for one who leaves wealth; altering it is a sin; Death or Sheol has gates (sha'arei mavet).

Shared motifs, rarest first: A king receives a foreign ruler's envoys and gift [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps and the Babylonian envoys: The king proudly shows foreign envoys all his treasures, prompting a prophecy of their loss; A cake of figs laid on a boil heals the king; Given a choice of signs, the king picks the harder (shadow going backward); Prophet tells the sick king 'Set your house in order, for you shall die'; King accepts doom for his descendants, glad there will be peace and truth in his own days; Dying man turns his face to the wall and prays, weeping; Prophecy that the king's descendants will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon; King makes a pool and conduit to bring water into the city; In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life; In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life [contrast between the texts]; As a sign the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway (dial) of Ahaz; God defends the city for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant; and 1 more.

Only in Solomon, the speech of birds, the ants, the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba: Entering Solomon's palace, the queen takes its floor of smooth glass for a pool and bares her legs; The hoopoe returns with sure news from Sabaʾ, knowledge Solomon lacked; Solomon sends the hoopoe to drop his letter before the queen and wait for their reply; Solomon reviews the birds, finds the hoopoe absent and threatens to punish or slaughter it unless it brings a clear excuse; An ʿifrīt of the jinn offers to bring the queen's throne before Solomon rises from his seat; Solomon's letter begins 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' and demands submission; The queen sends a gift to see what the envoys bring back; Solomon rejects the wealth and threatens invasion; The queen confesses she wronged herself and submits with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds; Solomon has the queen's throne disguised to test whether she recognizes it; she says 'It is as though it were it'; The queen and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God; Solomon inherits from David (knowledge and kingship); Solomon prays to be inspired to thank God for favor to him and his parents and to be admitted among the righteous; and 22 more.

title: Josiah's temple repair, the finding of the book and Huldah's oracle ↔ Temple repair, finding of the book of the Torah, Huldah's oracle and covenant
summary: These two units share 5 motifs: a lost book of the law is found in the temple during repairs, royal officials consult a woman prophet on behalf of the king, because the king humbled himself, he will die in peace and not see the coming disaster, workmen handling sacred funds are not audited because they deal faithfully….

title: Josiah's covenant, purge of the cults and Passover; death at Megiddo ↔ The moving shadow, the night garment, the two seas and the constellations
summary: These two units share 1 motifs: worship of the constellations or zodiac signs (mazzalot).

passages.note: Worship of the constellations or zodiac signs (mazzalot)
passages.text: וְהִשְׁבִּ֣ית אֶת הַכְּמָרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָֽתְנוּ֙ מַלְכֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה וַיְקַטֵּ֤ר בַּבָּמוֹת֙ בְּעָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה וּמְסִבֵּ֖י יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְאֶת הַֽמְקַטְּרִ֣ים לַבַּ֗עַל לַשֶּׁ֤מֶשׁ וְלַיָּרֵ֨חַ֙ וְלַמַּזָּל֔וֹת וּלְכֹ֖ל צְבָ֥א הַשָּׁמָֽיִם

passages.note: Worship of the constellations or zodiac signs (mazzalot) (burūj as God's work, not objects of worship)

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Worship of the constellations or zodiac signs (mazzalot) (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Josiah's covenant, purge of the cults and Passover; death at Megiddo: Idolatrous cult objects are burned and their dust carried away or thrown on graves; Despite the righteous king's reform, God does not turn from his anger over a predecessor's sins; Horses dedicated to the sun at the temple entrance and chariots of the sun burned; The high places Solomon built on the 'mount of destruction' (Mount of Olives) for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom; The righteous king is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necho; Priests of the high places are slaughtered on their own altars; An old prophecy (naming the future king) is fulfilled generations later; The bones of a prophet are left undisturbed when other graves are desecrated; Priests of the high places may not serve at the altar but eat unleavened bread among their brothers; The Tophet in the valley of Ben-hinnom is defiled so no one may burn children to Molech; A Passover such as had not been kept since the days of the judges; Women weave 'houses' (garments, hangings) for Asherah in the temple precinct; and 11 more.

Only in The moving shadow, the night garment, the two seas and the constellations: God extends the shadow, makes the sun its guide, then draws it back gently; God created humans from water and gave them kinship by blood and by marriage; Told to prostrate to the Merciful, the pagans ask 'What is al-Raḥmān?'; What God does after creating in six days [divergence between the texts]; God has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness; God made the night a garment, sleep a rest, and the day a rising (nushūr); As a sign the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway (dial) of Ahaz; God set constellations (buruj) in the sky and adorned it for beholders; God the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-hayy al-qayyum); God let loose the two seas, one sweet, one salt, with a barrier (barzakh) and partition between them; God makes winds his messengers (angels) and flaming fire his ministers; A solid firmament (raqia) separates upper waters from lower waters; and 6 more.

title: The siege and destruction of Jerusalem; Gedaliah; Jehoiachin released ↔ Historical appendix: siege, burning of the temple, bronze spoils, deportation numbers, Jehoiachin's release

Only in Jehoram's campaign against Mesha of Moab: Besieged king offers his firstborn heir as a burnt offering on the city wall, and 'great wrath' falls on Israel, who withdraw; Prophet calls for a musician; as he plays, the hand of YHWH comes upon him; Prophet says he would not even look at the wicked king were it not for the righteous ally; Invaders fell every good tree, stop every spring and ruin every good field with stones; Allied kings on a seven-day detour run out of water for army and beasts and despair; A sheep-breeding vassal king pays tribute of a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams; At sunrise the water looks red as blood; the enemy thinks the kings have slain each other and rushes to plunder; Dry wadi fills with water though no wind or rain is seen; Standard regnal formula: age at accession, length of reign, mother's name, evaluation, burial, successor; Nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods.

Only in Al-Hashr: the first gathering and exile of the Banu Nadir, the cut palms, and the law of fay': The expelled demolish their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers; Had God not decreed exile (jala') for them, he would have punished them in this world; God expelled the unbelieving People of the Book (the Banu Nadir) from their homes at 'the first gathering' (li-awwal al-hashr); Whatever palm trees (lina) you cut down or left standing on their roots was by God's leave; Later believers pray: forgive us and our brethren who preceded us in faith, and put no rancor in our hearts; Whether the enemy's trees may be cut down in a siege [contrast between the texts]; How spoil taken from the enemy is distributed [divergence between the texts]; Fay' (booty gained without cavalry or camels) goes to God, the messenger, kin, orphans, the poor and the wayfarer, so wealth does not circulate only among the rich; They thought their fortresses would protect them from God, but God came from where they did not expect and cast terror into their hearts; The poor emigrants and the hosts who prefer others over themselves even in need; whoever is saved from his own greed succeeds; Cities 'great and fortified up to heaven'; Spoils divided half to warriors, half to community, with a levy for God; and 2 more.

passages.note: David's repentance and what follows it [divergence between the texts] (Verdict, recognition and outcome. Sam: David burns with anger, ben-māweṯ hā-ʾîš, fourfold restitution; Nathan: ʾattâ hā-ʾîš; David: ḥāṭāʾṯî la-YHWH; pardon with a penalty, gam ha-bbēn ha-yyillôḏ ləḵā môṯ yāmûṯ, and the sword never leaves his house (12:10). Q: a calm verdict, la-qad ẓalamaka bi-suʾāli naʿjatika ilā niʿājihi; no 'you are the man'. David himself perceives (ẓanna Dāwūdu annamā fatannāhu) that it was a test, fa-staghfara rabbahu wa-kharra rākiʿan wa-anāb, and then fa-ghafarnā lahu dhālika wa-inna lahu ʿindanā la-zulfā wa-ḥusna maʾāb. evidence.text: Passages are shown for the 10 rarest of 16 shared motifs; the full list follows.

Shared motifs, rarest first: God rewards the speaker according to his righteousness and clean hands (weight 6.7); 'By my God I leap over a wall' (weight 6.7); God trains the king's hands for war so his arms bend a bow of bronze (weight 6.7); God shows steadfast love to his anointed and his seed forever (weight 6.7); Enemies beaten fine as dust and trampled like mire of the streets (weight 6.7); God reaches from on high and draws the sufferer out of many waters (weight 6.7); Foreigners come cringing and trembling to submit to the king (weight 6.7); Smoke rises from God's nostrils and devouring fire from his mouth (weight 6.7); God hears the cry from his (heavenly) temple (weight 6.7); God shows himself loyal to the loyal and crooked to the crooked (weight 6.7); God rides on a cherub and flies on the wings of the wind (weight 6.7); God is called the speaker's lamp who lights his darkness (weight 6.3); God makes the speaker's feet like hinds' feet and sets him on the heights (weight 6.3); The psalmist is engulfed by breakers of death and cords of Sheol (weight 6.3); God shoots his arrows at the people or enemies (weight 5.6); At God's coming the earth quakes, heavens drip and mountains flow (weight 5.2). Pair score 103.2.

Only in David's song of deliverance (= Psalm 18): Leader and people sing a victory song after the enemy's destruction; Theophany with thunder, lightning, thick cloud and a loud trumpet; God called the Rock (tsur).

Only in Psalm 18 - David's song of deliverance and the storm theophany: God makes darkness his hiding place and dark waters and clouds his canopy; The king gives thanks for God's deliverance from all his enemies (song also in 2 Sam 22); At God's rebuke the channels of the sea are seen and the foundations of the world laid bare; 'Who is God except YHWH, and who is a rock besides our God?'; God answers the distressed when he calls and removes the evil; God's words are pure, silver refined in a furnace, purified seven times; God addressed with a string of protective epithets: rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of salvation, stronghold; God sends hail mingled with fire and thunder from heaven; Thunder is the roaring voice of God; On that day a great earthquake shakes the land; fish, birds, beasts, creeping things and all humans quake before God, mountains are thrown down and every wall falls; Superscription sets the psalm in a specific episode of David's life.

Only in The last words of David: A just ruler is like the morning sun on a cloudless day; Poem opening with 'Oracle (ne'um) of the man...' formula; The spirit of God speaks through the king's tongue; The wicked are thorns that cannot be handled and are burned; God has made an everlasting covenant with the king's house.

Only in The chain of revelation; Jesus, word and spirit; 'say not three': The angels brought near (al-muqarrabūn) to God; God spoke to Moses directly (kallama taklīman); Jesus is God's word cast to Mary and a spirit from him; Catalogue of prophets who received revelation, from Noah to Jesus; People of the Book, do not go to excess (lā taghlū) in your religion; The Messiah does not disdain to be a servant of God, nor do the angels brought near; Do not say 'three'; God is only one god (rejection of a triad); First servant song: God's chosen servant with his spirit brings justice to the nations without crying out; a bruised reed he will not break; Of the messengers before you, some we have related to you and some we have not; God speaks to the prophet face to face, as a man speaks to his friend; Whether God has a son, or calls his anointed king his begotten son [contrast between the texts]; Denial that God has taken a son (walad); and 2 more.

Aramaic ṣidqâ ('righteousness', here almsgiving) and Arabic ṣadaqa. Daniel advises a pagan king; the Quran makes it a rule for believers and prefers secret giving.

Only in Owner of sovereignty: On the day each soul finds what good and evil it did present before it, wishing a far distance from its evil; Believers may not take unbelievers as allies, unless guarding against them (tuqat); God warns you of himself (yuhadhdhirukum allahu nafsahu); God makes night enter day and day night, brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living; O God, owner of sovereignty, you give it to whom you will and take it from whom you will; you exalt and abase; God changes times and seasons, deposes kings and sets up kings; God gives justice to the poor and seats kings (or the lowly) on the throne; God provides for whom he wills without reckoning (bi-ghayri hisab); Hymn of reversals: the barren bears seven, the mighty broken, the poor raised from the dung-heap.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/01-hb-quran.yaml): parallel. Cognate pair of titles: Dan 6:27 dî hûʾ ʾĕlāhāʾ ḥayyāʾ wĕ-qayyām lĕ-ʿālmîn 'the living God, enduring forever'; Q 2:255 allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa l-ḥayyu l-qayyūm. Aramaic ḥayyāʾ wĕ-qayyām = Arabic al-ḥayy al-qayyūm. In Daniel the title is spoken by a pagan king's decree; in the Quran it opens the Throne Verse.
Shared motifs, rarest first: Israel's God is called 'the living God, enduring forever, whose kingdom shall never be destroyed' (weight 6.3). Pair score 6.3.

Only in Daniel in the lions' den: The accusers, with their wives and children, are thrown to the lions and crushed before they reach the bottom; God sends his angel and shuts the lions' mouths so they do not harm the innocent; For thirty days no one may petition any god or man except the king; Darius the Mede receives the kingdom at age sixty-two; A stone is placed on the mouth of the pit and sealed with the king's signet and those of his nobles; A royal decree written by the law of the Medes and Persians cannot be revoked, even by the king; The king spends a sleepless night fasting, without entertainment, worrying over the hero; The pious kneels on his knees to pray; The faithful prays facing Jerusalem through open windows; Rivals can find no fault in the hero except in the matter of the law of his God; The king appoints 120 satraps over the kingdom with three presidents above them, one of them the hero; The hero is thrown into a pit of lions; and 8 more.

Only in Ranks of the messengers and the Throne Verse: God's footstool or seat (kursi) extends over the heavens and the earth; No compulsion in religion; Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes God; God's throne in relation to heaven and earth [divergence between the texts]; Whoever rejects false gods (taghut) and believes in God grasps the firmest handhold that never breaks; God does not slumber or sleep [divergence between the texts]; The guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps; A day comes with no trade, no friendship and no intercession; The temple as a house of rest for the ark and the footstool of God's feet; Jesus son of Mary given clear signs and supported with the holy spirit (ruh al-qudus); God ranked some messengers above others; to some God spoke; God the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-hayy al-qayyum); and 4 more.

passages.note: One mighty in power (shadid al-quwa) taught him, stood poised on the highest horizon, then drew near and descended (A heavenly being flies down to a praying man to instruct him: wə-hā-ʾîš gaḇrîʾēl ... muʿāp̄ bîʿāp̄ nōḡēaʿ ʾēlay ... wa-yyāḇen wa-yḏabbēr ʿimmî ... yāṣāʾṯî lə-haśkîləḵā ḇînâ vs. ʿallamahu shadīdu l-quwā dhū mirratin fa-stawā wa-huwa bi-l-ufuqi l-aʿlā thumma danā fa-tadallā ... fa-awḥā ilā ʿabdihi mā awḥā. Daniel names him Gabriel; Q 53 does not name the 'mighty in power' (tradition identifies him as Jibrīl, cf. Q 2:97). Daniel's angel explains a vision; the Quran's figure transmits revelation (waḥy).)

A heavenly being flies down to a praying man to instruct him: wə-hā-ʾîš gaḇrîʾēl ... muʿāp̄ bîʿāp̄ nōḡēaʿ ʾēlay ... wa-yyāḇen wa-yḏabbēr ʿimmî ... yāṣāʾṯî lə-haśkîləḵā ḇînâ vs. ʿallamahu shadīdu l-quwā dhū mirratin fa-stawā wa-huwa bi-l-ufuqi l-aʿlā thumma danā fa-tadallā ... fa-awḥā ilā ʿabdihi mā awḥā. Daniel names him Gabriel; Q 53 does not name the 'mighty in power' (tradition identifies him as Jibrīl, cf. Q 2:97). Daniel's angel explains a vision; the Quran's figure transmits revelation (waḥy).
Shared motifs, rarest first: One mighty in power (shadid al-quwa) taught him, stood poised on the highest horizon, then drew near and descended (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Daniel's penitential prayer and the seventy weeks: The angel arrives in swift flight at the time of the evening offering, while the seer is still praying; An anointed one (mashiah) is cut off and has nothing; The curse and oath written in the Torah of Moses has been poured out on the people; Communal confession: 'To you, Lord, belongs righteousness and to us shame of face'; We present our pleas not because of our righteous deeds but because of your great mercy; The seer studies the books (sefarim) to understand a prophecy; Seventy 'weeks' (seventy sevens) decreed to finish transgression, atone iniquity, bring everlasting righteousness and anoint a most holy; The seer is addressed as 'greatly beloved' (ish hamudot); Prayer accompanied by fasting, sackcloth and ashes; Muhammad is not the father of any of your men but the messenger of God and the seal of the prophets (khatam al-nabiyyin); An abomination that makes desolate (shiqquts meshomem) is set up in the sanctuary; The angel Gabriel is named and sent to explain the vision; and 3 more.

Only in Al-Najm: the star that sets, the mighty one on the horizon two bow-lengths away, and the Lote-Tree of the Boundary: The heart did not falsify what it saw; the gaze did not swerve nor transgress; When there covered the Lote-Tree that which covered it (an ineffable phenomenon); Oath 'By the star when it sets/falls (idha hawa)'; He saw him at a second descent by the Lote-Tree of the Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha), near the Garden of Refuge; The heavenly figure came within two bow-lengths or nearer (qaba qawsayn aw adna) and revealed to his servant; Leaders see God with a sapphire-like pavement under his feet; He saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord; Your companion has not erred; he does not speak from desire; it is only revelation revealed; Whether a prophet speaks from his own heart or desire, or by revelation [contrast between the texts]; What or whom the visionaries saw: God himself or his messenger [divergence between the texts]; No human can see God's face and live; A tree whose fruit gives eternal life.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/08-hb-quran.yaml): echo. wa-jibrīlu wa-ṣāliḥu l-muʾminīna wa-l-malāʾikatu baʿda dhālika ẓahīr ~ we-hā-ʾîš Gavrîʾēl ʾăšer rāʾîtî ve-ḥāzôn. The only named angel shared by both books; in Daniel he comes to explain the vision, in Q 66:4 he is the prophet's ally (ẓahīr) in a household dispute.
Shared motifs, rarest first: The angel Gabriel is named and sent to explain the vision (weight 6.0). Pair score 6.0.

Only in Daniel's penitential prayer and the seventy weeks: The angel arrives in swift flight at the time of the evening offering, while the seer is still praying; An anointed one (mashiah) is cut off and has nothing; The curse and oath written in the Torah of Moses has been poured out on the people; Communal confession: 'To you, Lord, belongs righteousness and to us shame of face'; We present our pleas not because of our righteous deeds but because of your great mercy; The seer studies the books (sefarim) to understand a prophecy; Seventy 'weeks' (seventy sevens) decreed to finish transgression, atone iniquity, bring everlasting righteousness and anoint a most holy; The seer is addressed as 'greatly beloved' (ish hamudot); Prayer accompanied by fasting, sackcloth and ashes; One mighty in power (shadid al-quwa) taught him, stood poised on the highest horizon, then drew near and descended; Muhammad is not the father of any of your men but the messenger of God and the seal of the prophets (khatam al-nabiyyin); An abomination that makes desolate (shiqquts meshomem) is set up in the sanctuary; and 3 more.

Only in Al-Tahrim: the prohibited thing and the divulged secret; fire fed with stones; the wives of Noah and Lot, Pharaoh's wife and Mary daughter of 'Imran: If he divorced them, God might give him in exchange better wives: submitting, believing, devout, repentant, worshipping, fasting/wandering (sa'ihat), previously married and virgins; A Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are harsh, stern angels who never disobey God; If two wives back each other against him, God is his protector, and Gabriel, the righteous believers and the angels; Mary, daughter of 'Imran, guarded her chastity; God breathed into it of his spirit, and she believed the words of her Lord and his books; Pharaoh's wife prays 'My Lord, build me a house with you in the Garden and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds'; The believers pray on the day: 'Our Lord, perfect our light for us and forgive us'; 'O Prophet, why do you forbid what God made lawful for you, seeking to please your wives?'; God has ordained the dissolution of oaths; Turn to God in sincere repentance (tawba nasuh); The prophet confided a secret to one of his wives; she divulged it, and God informed him; The wives of Noah and Lot, married to righteous servants, betrayed them and are told to enter the Fire; Father or husband may annul a woman's vow on the day he hears it; A man's vow or oath must be fulfilled as uttered [contrast between the texts]; and 10 more.

title: Setting of Moses' speech; appointment of judges ↔ Ha-Mim 'Ayn-Sin-Qaf: revelation, the angels' intercession and the one religion of the prophets
summary: These two units share 1 motifs: judges must not show partiality, 'for the judgment is god's'.

passages.note: Judges must not show partiality, 'for the judgment is God's'
passages.text: וָאֲצַוֶּה֙ אֶת שֹׁ֣פְטֵיכֶ֔ם בָּעֵ֥ת הַהִ֖וא לֵאמֹ֑ר שָׁמֹ֤עַ בֵּין אֲחֵיכֶם֙ וּשְׁפַטְתֶּ֣ם צֶ֔דֶק בֵּֽין אִ֥ישׁ וּבֵין אָחִ֖יו וּבֵ֥ין גֵּרֽוֹ

passages.note: Judges must not show partiality, 'for the judgment is God's'

passages.note: Judges must not show partiality, 'for the judgment is God's' (whatever you differ over, its judgment is God's)
passages.text: وَمَا ٱخْتَلَفْتُمْ فِيهِ مِن شَىْءٍ فَحُكْمُهُۥٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ ذَٰلِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّى عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ وَإِلَيْهِ أُنِيبُ

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Judges must not show partiality, 'for the judgment is God's' (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Setting of Moses' speech; appointment of judges: Eleven days' journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea (yet it took forty years); People multiplied 'like the stars of heaven'; Moses 'expounds this Torah' in Moab on the first of the eleventh month of the fortieth year; Blessing: may God make you a thousand times as many; Officers over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens; hard cases to the leader; Leader protests he did not conceive or bear the people to carry them like a nurse; Ideal borders of the promised land traced from the Brook of Egypt to Lebo-Hamath; The defeat of Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan recalled.

Only in Ha-Mim 'Ayn-Sin-Qaf: revelation, the angels' intercession and the one religion of the prophets: Whoever seeks the tillage (harth) of the hereafter has it increased; whoever seeks the tillage of this world gets some of it and no share hereafter; Perhaps the Hour is near; unbelievers mock and ask to hasten it, believers fear it; The prophet's only requested 'wage' is affection among kin (al-mawadda fi l-qurba); 'There is nothing like him' (laysa ka-mithlihi shay'), yet he is the Hearing, the Seeing; Abraham kept God's charge, commandments, statutes and laws (torot) before Sinai; Angels glorify God and ask forgiveness for those on earth; God sent down the Book with the truth and the Balance (al-mizan); Earlier communities split into factions only after knowledge came to them, out of rivalry (baghy) among themselves; God expands provision (rizq) for whom he wills and restricts it; The heavens almost burst apart from above (at God's majesty or at a blasphemy); To God belong the keys (maqalid) of the heavens and the earth; Whether humans bear God's likeness, or nothing is like him [contrast between the texts]; and 11 more.

summary: These two units share 2 motifs: how many witnesses are required [divergence between the texts], no one put to death on the testimony of a single witness.

passages.note: How many witnesses are required [divergence between the texts] (Deut 17:6 ʿal pî šĕnayim ʿēdîm ʾô šĕlōšâ ʿēdîm yûmat ha-mmēt: two or three witnesses for a capital case; Q 4:15 fa-stashhidū ʿalayhinna arbaʿatan minkum: four witnesses required for a charge of indecency (fāḥisha). passages.note: Limits on how many wives the leader may take [divergence between the texts] (A limit on the leader's wives. Deut: wə-lōʾ yarbeh-lô nāšîm wə-lōʾ yāsûr ləḇāḇô, a general cap on number, for fear his heart turns. Q: first an enumerated permission (innā aḥlalnā laka azwājaka ... khāliṣatan laka min dūni l-muʾminīn), then a freeze: lā yaḥillu laka n-nisāʾu min baʿdu wa-lā an tabaddala bihinna min azwājin wa-law aʿjabaka ḥusnuhunna. Deut does not let the number grow; the Quran grants a special privilege and then closes it.)

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): contrast, divergence. Both punish man and woman alike, but differently: û-mētû gam šənêhem hā-ʾîš ... wə-hā-ʾiššâ ~ az-zāniyatu wa-z-zānī fa-jlidū kulla wāḥidin minhumā miʾata jaldatin: death in Deuteronomy, a hundred lashes in the Quran. Note also the order: the Quran names the woman first. Punishing the false accuser of a woman: Deut 22:18-19 the husband who brought out an evil name (hôṣîʾ šēm rāʿ) is chastised (wə-yissərû ʾōtô), fined a hundred silver and may never divorce her; Q 24:4 anyone who accuses chaste women (al-muḥṣanāt) without four witnesses gets eighty lashes, and his testimony is never accepted again. In the Quran the husband's case goes to the oath procedure of 24:6-9.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Husband who falsely accuses his bride is flogged, fined 100 silver, and may never divorce her (weight 6.7); The penalty for adultery or fornication [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.7); The penalty for falsely accusing a woman of unchastity [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); Adulterer and adulteress both put to death (weight 6.3). Pair score 26.4.
